subtype: Approach: assigns one member to question the plan [Revision]
passage:
Faculty advisor's note, cultural fest committee.
This week the committee tried something new. At the start of each meeting one member is named the devil's advocate, and the only job is to question the plan. Today it was Baljeet's turn. Baljeet asked one plain thing: "Where does the money for moving the stage come from?"
Nobody had an answer. Two members checked the sheet and found that the budget had no line for transport. There was some groaning, but the gap was found nine days before the fest, not on the day.
I did nothing except suggest they rotate the role. Next week someone else takes the turn.
Sonali

qa.q: How many days before the fest was the gap found?
qa.a: The gap was found nine days before the fest.

qa.q: What might the committee members have felt when nobody could answer Baljeet's question?
qa.a: They probably felt surprised and a bit embarrassed, shown by the groaning, but also relieved to find the gap early.

qa.q: What could the committee do to keep the role useful in coming weeks?
qa.a: They could keep rotating the devil's advocate and ask the questions in writing beforehand, so each meeting checks a different part of the plan.

qa.q: How does the faculty advisor see the new habit?
qa.a: The advisor kept out of it, only suggesting the role rotate, which suggests trust that the students' own questions are working.

grounding: A student team names a devil's advocate at each meeting, and the questions reveal a budget gap before it becomes a problem.

subtype: Approach: goes along with the group because no one wants to disagree [Pitfall]
passage:
Monday. In the launch meeting Ankita, the team lead, says, "We go live on the 15th." It is ten days away. Uday looks at the testing list, still half open, and says nothing. Two others glance at their laptops. "Great," says Ankita. "Everyone's on board."
Thursday. Uday, in a chat with a colleague: "Are you sure about the 15th?" "No. But nobody is saying anything." "I'm not going to be the one."
The 16th. The page is not ready. Ankita calls a meeting, surprised. "Why didn't anyone say it was too tight?" Nobody speaks for a moment. Uday looks at the table.

qa.q: On which date did Ankita want to go live?
qa.a: Ankita said the team would go live on the 15th.

qa.q: What was Uday feeling in the launch meeting?
qa.a: Uday felt doubtful about the date, seeing the half-open testing list, but too uneasy to speak up.

qa.q: What could Uday or the others do next time they doubt a date?
qa.a: One of them could raise the open testing list politely at the meeting, since a shared doubt stays hidden when everyone waits for someone else.

qa.q: How might Ankita feel on the 16th?
qa.a: Ankita is surprised and probably disappointed, having thought everyone was on board when several had doubts.

grounding: A team agrees to an unrealistic launch date because the leader is keen, doubters stay silent, and the date is missed.

subtype: Approach: collects opinions privately before discussion [Revision]
passage:
Tuesday. Ramesh, the manager, sends a message before the planning meeting: "Please email me your honest concerns about the new schedule by tonight. Don't discuss it with others first."
Wednesday. Before the meeting, Ramesh reads eight replies. Hemant, the newest member, wrote: "The Friday deadline clashes with the supplier's holiday." Two of the senior members had not seen it. In the meeting, Ramesh reads out the concerns without names.
The following Monday. The schedule now has a Thursday deadline. Hemant tells a friend at lunch, "I would never have said that in the room with everyone there."

qa.q: How many replies did Ramesh read before the meeting?
qa.a: Ramesh read eight replies before the meeting.

qa.q: What does Hemant feel about sharing the concern in writing?
qa.a: Hemant feels relieved and safer, since Hemant would never have said it in the room with everyone there.

qa.q: What else could Ramesh do to make sure quiet members are heard?
qa.a: Ramesh could ask each person for one written concern before every big meeting, since it keeps seniors' words from shaping the views of others.

qa.q: How might the senior members see the concern from Hemant?
qa.a: Two of the senior members had not seen the clash with the holiday, so may be grateful that it came up before the schedule was fixed.

grounding: A manager asks for written views before the meeting so junior concerns appear without being shaped by senior voices.

subtype: Approach: invites an outsider to review the plan [Action]
passage:
Jaya here. When we finished the launch plan for our new leave-request page, everyone on the team felt good about it. So we did something a little uncomfortable: we asked Lalremsiami from the finance department to read it. I sent her the plan with a short note, asking her to mark anything that looked odd.
Two days later she came back with one line circled. Our plan said, "Staff will see the launch email on Monday morning." She asked, "What about people on the night shift or the plant floor, who don't open email at a desk?"
None of us had thought of it. We had all assumed everyone reads email at a desk. We added notices at the gate and a short talk at shift change.

qa.q: Which line did Lalremsiami circle?
qa.a: She circled the line that said staff will see the launch email on Monday morning.

qa.q: How did Jaya's team feel about the plan before it was reviewed?
qa.a: The team felt good and confident about the plan, which is why nobody had spotted the shared assumption.

qa.q: What could the team do next time before a launch?
qa.a: They could again ask someone from another department to read the plan, since an outsider does not share the team's assumptions.

qa.q: How might people on the night shift see the launch after the change?
qa.a: They would now see notices at the gate and hear a talk at shift change, so they would not miss the launch just because they don't open email at a desk.

grounding: The team asks a colleague from another department to read the launch plan, and she spots an assumption everyone had shared.

subtype: Approach: uses trial and error for a small new puzzle [Thinking]
passage:
I'm Indu. Tushar lives next door, and yesterday Tushar found a board game in a box with no rule sheet. Nobody in that house knew how to play it. I expected Tushar to give up, but Tushar just started moving the pieces.
"If I move this one, does it stop?" Tushar said. "Oh, it can't go there. Okay, not that way." Then a card: "Ha, this one sends me back." Every time something went wrong there was a laugh and another try.
I don't know if there was a plan. It looked like working it out as the game went along, and it looked like fun.

qa.q: Where did Tushar find the board game?
qa.a: Tushar found it in a box with no rule sheet.

qa.q: What might Tushar have been feeling while trying the moves?
qa.a: Tushar seemed curious and cheerful, laughing at each mistake, though Indu cannot be sure what Tushar was thinking.

qa.q: What could Tushar do if the game got too confusing to work out?
qa.a: Tushar could ask an older person or look for the rules, since trial and error suits a small puzzle but a stuck game may need help.

qa.q: How does Indu see Tushar's way of learning the game?
qa.a: Indu expected Tushar to give up, but saw a person working it out and having fun, so was a bit surprised.

grounding: A boy facing a new board game with no rules just tries moves and sees what happens, since mistakes cost nothing.

subtype: Approach: asks an adult when the problem is unsafe or too big [Thinking]
passage:
I'm Aparna, and I was at Deepika's house when it happened. We were in the garden looking for a lost ball when Deepika went very still. "Snake," Deepika whispered. It was long and brown, near the water tap.
I wanted to look closer, but Deepika pulled me back. "Too big for us. Papa will know what to do." Deepika ran inside and came back with Papa, who told us to stand on the veranda. He called a person who helps with snakes, and we watched from the steps until the helper came.
Deepika's hands shook a little, but Deepika kept saying, "We didn't touch it."

qa.q: Where was the snake?
qa.a: The snake was long and brown, near the water tap in the garden.

qa.q: What was Deepika feeling when standing very still in the garden?
qa.a: Deepika felt frightened, seen in the whisper and shaking hands, but also careful about staying safe.

qa.q: Which choice worked here, and why?
qa.a: Calling Papa worked, because the snake was too big for the children and an adult could call a person who helps with snakes.

qa.q: What was it like for Aparna to be pulled back?
qa.a: Aparna wanted to look closer, so may have felt curious and a little held back, but stayed safe on the veranda steps.

grounding: A child who finds a snake in the garden calls Papa and does not try to deal with it alone.

subtype: Approach: uses a checklist for a familiar routine task [Thinking]
passage:
Asif, class eleven. Our school has a trip every term, and for three years I have packed the same way: from a list. It's on a card in my drawer: ID card, water bottle, charger, two pens, raincoat, sun hat, snacks.
The night before a trip I lay everything on the bed, tick it off, then zip the bag. It takes ten minutes, and I don't have to think. My sister Zainab laughs at the card, but last term she forgot her ID card and had to phone home from the gate.
A list works because the job is always the same. For something new I'd need more than a card.

qa.q: What is on the card in Asif's drawer?
qa.a: The card lists an ID card, water bottle, charger, two pens, raincoat, sun hat and snacks.

qa.q: How does Asif feel about packing from the list?
qa.a: Asif feels comfortable and untroubled, since it takes ten minutes and there is no need to think.

qa.q: What could Asif do if the trip were a new kind, such as a camp?
qa.a: Asif could ask the teacher what to bring and write a new list, since the old card fits only the same repeated job.

qa.q: How might Zainab feel about laughing at the card, then forgetting the ID?
qa.a: Zainab may feel a bit embarrassed at having to phone home from the gate, and may see the card as more useful than she thought.

grounding: A student who packs for similar school trips uses a fixed list because a repeated task with known steps is faster than fresh thinking.

subtype: Approach: makes a careful plan when the stakes are high [Thinking]
passage:
I'm Harish, and I sat behind Samir in class during the scholarship weeks. Samir wrote every step on the back of a notebook: certificates, the income form, the essay, the last date.
On Tuesday I saw Samir laying out the papers and going through them a second time, line by line. Then Samir took the essay to Mrs Deshmukh, the maths teacher, who read it and circled two spelling errors and a wrong date.
"It's a big form," Samir told me. "If I make a mistake, I can't change it after." I asked why not just send it. Samir said, "It isn't like a class test." The form went in two days before the deadline.

qa.q: Who read Samir's essay?
qa.a: Mrs Deshmukh, the maths teacher, read the essay.

qa.q: Why did Samir check the papers twice, in Samir's own words?
qa.a: Samir felt worried about a mistake that cannot be changed, and said a big form is not like a class test.

qa.q: What could Samir add to the plan if there were even more time?
qa.a: Samir could ask a second person to read the form fresh, since a new reader may catch errors that Samir and the teacher missed.

qa.q: How might Mrs Deshmukh see the request to review the essay?
qa.a: Mrs Deshmukh was asked to read something important, and by finding a wrong date and two errors was clearly useful, so may feel glad to have helped.

grounding: A teenager applying for a scholarship plans each step, checks documents twice and asks a teacher to review because errors here are costly.

subtype: Approach: asks an expert when the problem is outside his knowledge [Thinking]
passage:
Coach's note, athletics club.
Vedant came to me after Thursday's practice with a question: his knee felt sore after sprints, and should he keep training? He said he had read three different answers online and they all disagreed.
I told him I could plan his sessions, but a question about a sore knee was one for a doctor, and I would not guess. I asked him to watch from the side that day and to tell his mother.
On Saturday he told me he had booked a visit with Dr Dilnaz and would bring me whatever she said about training. I have put the knee question on hold until then.
Irawati, coach

qa.q: How many different answers had Vedant read online?
qa.a: Vedant had read three different answers online, and they all disagreed.

qa.q: What was Vedant likely worried about after practice?
qa.a: Vedant was worried about the sore knee and unsure whether to keep training, since the online answers disagreed.

qa.q: What could Vedant do if the doctor's advice changes the training plan?
qa.a: Vedant could share the doctor's words with the coach and let the coach adjust the sessions, since the coach plans training and the doctor answers questions about the knee.

qa.q: How might Vedant's mother feel after being told about the knee?
qa.a: She may feel concerned but also reassured that Vedant took the question to a coach and a doctor, not a random online answer.

grounding: A teenager with a health-related sports question asks a coach and a doctor instead of guessing from social media.

subtype: Approach: uses time-boxing when a task is dull and easy to postpone [Thinking]
passage:
Monday. Zubair looks at the chemistry practice sets and finds something else to do: pencil case, water, a text to Aditi about football. The pages stay shut.
Wednesday. Sitting near Aditi in the library, Zubair thinks, if it's only twenty-five minutes, I can stand it. He sets a phone alarm, puts the phone face down and opens the set. The first ten minutes drag. By the end, four questions are done, and the alarm sounds before he expects it.
Next Monday. Zubair takes out the sets and starts the timer without being asked. He does two rounds, then closes the book with a page marked. "It's still dull," he tells Aditi, "but it's only twenty-five minutes."

qa.q: How long is Zubair's timer set for?
qa.a: Zubair sets the alarm for twenty-five minutes.

qa.q: What was Zubair thinking before opening the chemistry set on Wednesday?
qa.a: Zubair thought that if it is only twenty-five minutes he could stand it, so felt the task was small enough to face.

qa.q: What could Zubair try if a twenty-five minute block still feels too long?
qa.a: Zubair could shorten it to a smaller block, since a bounded start is what helps him begin a task he tends to put off.

qa.q: How might Aditi see the change in Zubair's habits?
qa.a: Aditi sat nearby and heard Zubair say it's still dull, so may see the timer as a practical way to get a dull task done.

grounding: A student who avoids chemistry practice uses a twenty-five minute timer, since a small bounded start suits a task he puts off.
